However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how language models encode and recall time-specific information, focusing on whether there are specific attention heads dedicated to temporal knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads in language models that encode and recall time-specific knowledge, and shows that ablating them impairs temporal knowledge while leaving other capabilities intact.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Temporal Heads are crucial for temporal knowledge in LLMs, and targeting them can enable precise temporal updates without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal Heads, such as a15.h0 and a18.h3 in Llama2, are identified across multiple models and are crucial for temporal knowledge recall.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal effect on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated for both numerical (e.g., 'In 2004') and textual (e.g., 'In the year...') temporal conditions, indicating they encode a broad temporal dimension.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the activations of these heads, enabling targeted updates.
Backup Temporal Heads exist that can compensate when primary heads are ablated, ensuring model robustness.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs was constrained due to lack of temporal dependencies in options.
EAP-IG does not support models with Grouped-Query Attention, limiting analysis of models like Llama-3.
future_direction: Future work should focus on broader application for enhancing temporal reasoning and time-aware model alignment.
papers.abstract: While the ability of language models to elicit facts has been widely investigated, how they handle temporally changing facts remains underexplored. We discover Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that primarily handle temporal knowledge, through circuit analysis. We confirm that these heads are present across multiple models, though their specific locations may vary, and their responses differ depending on the type of knowledge and its corresponding years. Disabling these heads degrades the model's ability to recall time-specific knowledge while maintaining its general capabilities without compromising time-invariant and question-answering performances. Moreover, the heads are activated not only numeric conditions ("In 2004") but also textual aliases ("In the year ..."), indicating that they encode a temporal dimension beyond simple numerical representation. Furthermore, we expand the potential of our findings by demonstrating how temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the values of these heads.

papers.title: ParaScopes: What do Language Models Activations Encode About Future Text?
papers.research_question: Does a language model encode information about its likely future outputs within its internal representations? This is operationalized as the planningDecodability Hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ParaScopes, a framework of Residual Stream Decoders, and provides evidence that language models encode paragraph-scale planning information in their activations, decodable with a lookahead of about 5 tokens.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that language models encode paragraph-scale planning information in their activations, which can be partially decoded using ParaScopes, with planning signals concentrated in middle layers and updated at paragraph boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Paragraph-level planning information is decodable from residual stream activations, comparable to having 5-10 tokens of lookahead.
TAE ParaScope captures broad semantic signals (topic/subject), while Continuation ParaScope is more inconsistent but can sometimes reveal more specific details.
Planning signals are concentrated in the middle layers (approximately 60-80% of the model's depth).
Models update plans just-in-time at paragraph boundaries, with a sharp shift in information at the '\n\n' token.
Outline-level planning is weakly decodable, suggesting limited planning at longer horizons in the studied model.
papers.limitation:
The planning signals extracted may not be strictly causal to model performance.
Focus on short structured paragraphs and outlines, which may not generalize to domains like math, code, and chemistry.
Tests are primarily limited to one model (Llama 3.2 3B).
future_direction: Further research into understanding the degree to which the planning signals are strictly causal to model performance.
Extend the approach to different horizons and investigate how these mechanisms interact with factual correctness or stylistic consistency.
Investigate planning in models of various sizes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability studies in language models often investigate forward-looking representations of activations. However, as language models become capable of doing ever longer time horizon tasks, methods for understanding activations often remain limited to testing specific concepts or tokens. We develop a framework of Residual Stream Decoders as a method of probing model activations for paragraph-scale and document-scale plans. We test several methods and find information can be decoded equivalent to 5+ tokens of future context in small models. These results lay the groundwork for better monitoring of language models and better understanding how they might encode longer-term planning information.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in Mamba
papers.research_question: Does factual recall in the Mamba state space model exhibit locality similar to the patterns observed in autoregressive transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: Despite architectural differences, Mamba exhibits similar localization patterns for factual recall as transformers, and many interpretability methods developed for transformers can be adapted to Mamba.
papers.conclusion: Many interpretability methods from transformers can be adapted to Mamba, and factual recall in Mamba shows similar localization patterns, indicating architectural similarities in how different models store and recall facts.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patching in Mamba reveals high causal effects at early-middle layers (subject last token) and later layers (prompt last token), similar to transformers.
ROME editing can successfully insert facts in Mamba by modifying projection matrices, with Wo being the most effective.
The linearity of relation decoding (LRE) in Mamba is similar to transformers, with some relations being more linearly decodable than others.
Adapted attention knockout experiments show that Mamba propagates relation information in early layers and subject information in middle layers, similar to information flow in transformers.
There is a separation of roles between early-mid and later layers in Mamba for factual recall, analogous to findings in transformers.
papers.limitation: Performing attention knockout in Mamba is challenging due to the Conv+SSM operation, making it difficult to block specific edges like in transformers.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms of factual recall in the Mamba state space model. Our work is inspired by previous findings in autoregressive transformer language models suggesting that their knowledge recall is localized to particular modules at specific token locations; we therefore ask whether factual recall in Mamba can be similarly localized. To investigate this, we conduct four lines of experiments on Mamba. First, we apply causal tracing or interchange interventions to localize key components inside Mamba that are responsible for recalling facts, revealing that specific components within middle layers show strong causal effects at the last token of the subject, while the causal effect of intervening on later layers is most pronounced at the last token of the prompt, matching previous findings on autoregressive transformers. Second, we show that rank-one model editing methods can successfully insert facts at specific locations, again resembling findings on transformer LMs. Third, we examine the linearity of Mamba's representations of factual relations. Finally we adapt attention-knockout techniques to Mamba in order to dissect information flow during factual recall. We compare Mamba directly to a similar-sized autoregressive transformer LM and conclude that despite significant differences in architectural approach, when it comes to factual recall, the two architectures share many similarities.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Distribution Prompting: Understanding the Expressivity of Language Models Through the Next-Token Distributions They Can Produce
papers.research_question: What are the general properties of next-token probability distributions that can be easily elicited from language models through prompting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models find it easier to approximate next-token distributions with very low or high entropy, those containing outlier tokens, and that LM-generated distributions are easier to approximate than randomly constructed ones.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals general properties of LM expressiveness in approximating next-token distributions, highlighting which distributions are easier or harder to elicit, and provides a framework for future analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Approximation loss as a function of target entropy is unimodal, with moderate entropy distributions being the hardest to approximate.
Distributions with outlier tokens (tokens with much higher probability) are easier to approximate than those without.
LM-generated target distributions are easier to approximate than randomly constructed distributions with matched entropy.
These patterns hold across different model architectures and sizes, and even for randomly initialized models.
Soft prompt tuning yields better approximation than hard prompt tuning, with hybrid approaches in between.
papers.limitation:
The study depends on the investigation of different target probability distributions entirely from the perspective of entropy, which is still a minor step compared to the whole picture of understanding the expressiveness of LMs.
The initialization of the prompt tuning actually matters in approximating certain distributions, which is also worthy of research.
The root cause of the observed phenomenon remains unclear, warranting further investigation.
future_direction: Further exploration of LM distributional behavior and the design of interpretable models.
Investigation of the root cause of the difficulty in approximating moderate-entropy distributions.
Application of the proposed framework to explore model behaviors from new interpretability perspectives.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive neural language models (LMs) generate a probability distribution over tokens at each time step given a prompt. In this work, we attempt to systematically understand the probability distributions that LMs can produce, showing that some distributions are significantly harder to elicit than others. Specifically, for any target next-token distribution over the vocabulary, we attempt to find a prompt that induces the LM to output a distribution as close as possible to the target, using either soft or hard gradient-based prompt tuning. We find that (1) in general, distributions with very low or very high entropy are easier to approximate than those with moderate entropy; (2) among distributions with the same entropy, those containing ''outlier tokens'' are easier to approximate; (3) target distributions generated by LMs -- even LMs with different tokenizers -- are easier to approximate than randomly chosen targets. These results offer insights into the expressiveness of LMs and the challenges of using them as probability distribution proposers.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Entropy-Lens: Uncovering Decision Strategies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do token prediction dynamics (expansion and pruning strategies) in LLMs vary across model families, tasks, and output formats, and how do these strategies impact downstream performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Entropy-Lens, a method to distill token-space dynamics of the residual stream into low-dimensional entropy profiles, revealing family-specific, task-specific, and format-specific patterns in expansion and pruning strategies, with expansion usually being more critical for performance.
papers.conclusion: Entropy-Lens provides a low-dimensional, interpretable view of token prediction dynamics in LLMs, revealing systematic patterns in how models expand and prune candidate tokens, which are informative about model family, task, and format, thereby enhancing understanding of information processing across model depth.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy profiles are family-specific and invariant under depth rescaling, showing that larger models refine the same underlying decision process.
Entropy profiles are characteristic of task type (generative, syntactic, semantic) and output format (poem, scientific piece, chat log).
Expansion and pruning strategies have unequal impact on downstream performance, with the expansion strategy usually being more critical for maintaining accuracy.
Entropy profiles can distinguish between correct and incorrect answers in multiple-choice question answering (MMLU).
The method is model-agnostic and works across a wide range of model families and sizes without requiring gradients, fine-tuning, or auxiliary probes.
papers.limitation:
Lack of mechanistic understanding of which specific architectural components or training schemes play a causal role in shaping a particular entropy profile.
Unclear how different training stages (e.g., fine-tuning, RLHF) alter the relative importance of expansion and pruning phases for downstream performance.
Analysis confined to decoder-only Transformers; not yet extended to architectures with different information flow paradigms, such as ViTs or Mixture-of-Experts.
future_direction: Mechanistic understanding of which architectural components or training schemes cause specific entropy profiles.
Investigating how different training stages alter the relative importance of expansion and pruning strategies.
Extending the framework to other architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) or Mixture-of-Experts models.
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), each block operates on the residual stream to map input token sequences to output token distributions. However, most of the interpretability literature focuses on internal latent representations, leaving token-space dynamics underexplored. The high dimensionality and categoricity of token distributions hinder their analysis, as standard statistical descriptors are not suitable. We show that the entropy of logit-lens predictions overcomes these issues. In doing so, it provides a per-layer scalar, permutation-invariant metric. We introduce Entropy-Lens to distill the token-space dynamics of the residual stream into a low-dimensional signal. We call this signal the entropy profile. We apply our method to a variety of model sizes and families, showing that (i) entropy profiles uncover token prediction dynamics driven by expansion and pruning strategies; (ii) these dynamics are family-specific and invariant under depth rescaling; (iii) they are characteristic of task type and output format; (iv) these strategies have unequal impact on downstream performance, with the expansion strategy usually being more critical. Ultimately, our findings further enhance our understanding of the residual stream, enabling a granular assessment of how information is processed across model depth.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which components (attention heads, FFNs) contribute to solving factual knowledge tasks, and how do these circuits for factual knowledge evolve over the course of model training?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge representation evolves during LLM pre-training, showing that models initially rely on general-purpose components which later specialize, with attention heads exhibiting high turnover and FFNs remaining more stable.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights into the hierarchical learning process of LLMs, where general components form first and later diversify, with attention heads being highly adaptive and FFNs providing stable processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads show high turnover and dynamic role transitions, while FFNs are more stable throughout training.
Location-based relations (LOC) converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations (NAME).
LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.
Answer-specific attention heads demonstrate the highest turnover, indicating frequent role changes.
FFNs act as a steady processing backbone, with most remaining in general roles.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level and the use of alternative interpretability techniques like activation patching across all snapshots.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based factual relations.
The analysis uses a fixed activation threshold for role classification, which may introduce bias.
Only a subset of training snapshots was analyzed, leaving gaps in tracking role transitions.
Direct comparison with other model families (e.g., Pythia) was not feasible due to architectural differences preventing the use of IFRs.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
Expand analysis to other domains, multilingual settings, and ambiguous queries.
Investigate the long-term impact of component dynamics on fine-tuning, pruning, and continual learning.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability.In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training.We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific and examine their stability and transitions.Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover.We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training.Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than namebased relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics.These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.We release the code and data. 1

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: On the Effect of Uncertainty on Layer-wise Inference Dynamics
papers.research_question: How does uncertainty affect the inference dynamics of models, and does model competence affect the ability to adapt inference dynamics to uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that uncertainty does not significantly affect the inference dynamics of LLMs, as probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are aligned. It also provides preliminary evidence that more competent models may exhibit adaptive inference dynamics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit similar token probability dynamics and tend to commit to final decisions at specific layers largely independent of output uncertainty, but show potential for greater adaptability in inference dynamics as model competence increases.
papers.key_findings:
Probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are strongly aligned across layers, with abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers.
Prediction depth distributions are similar for correct and incorrect answers, indicating the model commits to its output at similar layers regardless of uncertainty.
Weak but consistent positive correlations exist between answer incorrectness and prediction depth across models and datasets.
Positive correlation between task proficiency (measured by Cohen's Kappa) and prediction depth difference suggests adaptive inference dynamics may emerge with greater model competence.
The findings challenge the feasibility of using simplistic methods for uncertainty detection at inference and suggest more nuanced interpretability approaches are needed.
papers.limitation:
The study is exploratory and requires further validation on more models, especially more competent ones.
More rigorous tests are needed, including analyses with varying levels of uncertainty and accounting for hallucination on known knowledge.
future_direction: Further testing on more models to validate the results, especially on more competent models.
More rigorous tests that include analyses using varying levels of uncertainty and accounts for hallucination on known knowledge.
Similar experiments for aleatoric uncertainty for a more thorough investigation.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) internally represent and process their predictions is central to detecting uncertainty and preventing hallucinations. While several studies have shown that models encode uncertainty in their hidden states, it is underexplored how this affects the way they process such hidden states. In this work, we demonstrate that the dynamics of output token probabilities across layers for certain and uncertain outputs are largely aligned, revealing that uncertainty does not seem to affect inference dynamics. Specifically, we use the Tuned Lens, a variant of the Logit Lens, to analyze the layer-wise probability trajectories of final prediction tokens across 11 datasets and 5 models. Using incorrect predictions as those with higher epistemic uncertainty, our results show aligned trajectories for certain and uncertain predictions that both observe abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers. We balance this finding by showing evidence that more competent models may learn to process uncertainty differently. Our findings challenge the feasibility of leveraging simplistic methods for detecting uncertainty at inference. More broadly, our work demonstrates how interpretability methods may be used to investigate the way uncertainty affects inference.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Contextual Representation Flow in State-Space and Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How does contextual information flow across layers in State Space Models (SSMs) and Transformer-Based Models (TBMs)?
papers.core_contribution: TBMs rapidly homogenize token representations early with diversity reemerging later, while SSMs preserve token uniqueness early but converge to homogenization deeper. Oversmoothing in TBMs stems from architectural design, whereas in SSMs it arises mainly from training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: TBMs and SSMs exhibit opposing oversmoothing trajectories: TBMs homogenize early then recover, while SSMs preserve early token uniqueness but converge to homogenization deeper.
papers.key_findings:
TBMs exhibit stable token evolution until a sharp final-layer shift, while SSMs show varied directional changes that converge in later layers.
TBMs collapse token distinctions early and recover diversity late, while SSMs maintain token uniqueness longer.
Oversmoothing in TBMs is an intrinsic architectural property, while in SSMs it is primarily a consequence of training.
Task-relevant representations peak in intermediate layers for both architectures, with SSMs having a smaller accuracy gap to the final layer than TBMs.
Despite stable representation evolution across context lengths, probing accuracy decreases as context length increases, indicating capacity limitations.
papers.limitation:
Cosine similarity is sensitive to parameterizations, biased by skip connections, and captures only local directional changes.
Findings are limited to the specific tasks (MDQA, KVPR) and models examined, which may limit generality.
future_direction: Extend the framework to multimodal domains such as video or speech.
Integrate similarity measures into the training loop for adaptive regularization schemes.
Explore hybrid architectures that combine the local retention of SSMs with the global reconfiguration capacity of TBMs.
papers.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have recently emerged as efficient alternatives to Transformer-Based Models (TBMs) for long-sequence processing with linear scaling, yet how contextual information flows across layers in these architectures remains understudied. We present the first unified, token- and layer-wise analysis of representation propagation in SSMs and TBMs. Using centered kernel alignment, variance-based metrics, and probing, we characterize how representations evolve within and across layers. We find a key divergence: TBMs rapidly homogenize token representations, with diversity reemerging only in later layers, while SSMs preserve token uniqueness early but converge to homogenization deeper. Theoretical analysis and parameter randomization further reveal that oversmoothing in TBMs stems from architectural design, whereas in SSMs, it arises mainly from training dynamics. These insights clarify the inductive biases of both architectures and inform future model and training designs for long-context reasoning.

papers.title: Autoregressive + Chain of Thought = Recurrent: Recurrence's Role in Language Models' Computability and a Revisit of Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: What are the distinct roles of recurrence and autoregression in neural models' computational power, and how does Chain of Thought (CoT) approximate recurrence to enhance reasoning capabilities in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that recurrence is crucial for computational depth in neural models, and that Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting approximates this missing recurrence in autoregressive Transformers by converting hidden states to text and back, thereby enhancing their computational capabilities. It also introduces the concept of 'recurrence-completeness' to analyze recurrent Transformer variants.
papers.conclusion: The analysis clarifies the roles of autoregression and recurrence, showing recurrence is key for computational depth. CoT approximates recurrence in Transformers, boosting their reasoning. The concept of recurrence-completeness reveals that some recurrent Transformer designs prioritize speed over computational power.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrence, not autoregression, is essential for increasing the depth complexity of neural models, enabling them to solve tasks requiring sequential computation.
Chain of Thought (CoT) mimics recurrence in Transformer-based LLMs by encoding hidden computational states into natural language tokens and decoding them back, acting as a bridge between autoregression and recurrence.
Empirical results show that CoT-enhanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) can solve tasks at Regular, Context-Free, and Context-Sensitive computational levels, whereas standard Transformers without CoT fail.
Some 'recurrent' Transformer designs (e.g., Linear Transformer, RWKV) are recurrence-incomplete and do not enhance computational power; they primarily aim for inference efficiency.
There is a trade-off between recurrence-completeness and parallel training: true recurrent models cannot be parallelized, while recurrence-incomplete models like Linear Transformers can.
papers.limitation:
Experimental task lengths are limited to under 20 elements to avoid issues with long-context retrieval and model errors unrelated to computability, which may limit generalizability to longer sequences.
The study uses only one LLM (GPT-4) for experiments, which may not represent all language models.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture excels in a variety of language modeling tasks, outperforming traditional neural architectures such as RNN and LSTM. This is partially due to its elimination of recurrent connections, which allows for parallel training and a smoother flow of gradients. However, this move away from recurrent structures places the Transformer model at the lower end of Chomsky's computational hierarchy, imposing limitations on its computational abilities. Consequently, even advanced Transformer-based models face considerable difficulties in tasks like counting, string reversal, and multiplication. These tasks, though seemingly elementary, require a level of computational complexity that exceeds the capabilities of the Transformer architecture. Concurrently, the emergence of ``Chain of Thought" (CoT) prompting has enabled Transformer-based language models to tackle tasks that were previously impossible or poorly executed. In this work, we thoroughly investigate the influence of recurrent structures in neural models on their reasoning abilities and computability, contrasting the role autoregression plays in the neural models' computational power. We then shed light on how the CoT approach can mimic recurrent computation and act as a bridge between autoregression and recurrence in the context of language models. It is this approximated recurrence that notably improves the model's performance and computational capacity. Moreover, we revisit recent recurrent-based Transformer model designs, focusing on their computational abilities through our proposed concept of ``recurrence-completeness" and identify key theoretical limitations in models like Linear Transformer and RWKV. Through this, we aim to provide insight into the neural model architectures and prompt better model design.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Interpreting Context Look-ups in Transformers: Investigating Attention-MLP Interactions
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly, providing a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads process context and use next-token neurons to help predict a word associated with, but not previously seen in that context, providing insight into how attention heads can work with MLP neurons to predict new words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can recognize contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron.
An automated method can explain and characterize interactions between attention heads and token-predicting neurons.
The head explanation score can be used to evaluate the quality of explanations.
The phenomenon is observed across different model families and sizes (GPT-2 and Pythia variants).
Ablation experiments confirm that the identified attention heads are causally involved in predicting the token.
papers.limitation:
Focus on max-activating behavior of neurons, which might overlook subtler activation patterns.
Reliance on a maximum of 30 prompts per neuron.
GPT-4 struggles with longer prompts and may generate poor explanations for certain patterns (like induction-style prompts).
Scope limited to neurons whose associated tokens are whole words and prompts shorter than 100 tokens.
future_direction: Investigate whether this phenomenon happens to such neurons throughout their range of activations.
Look into whether multiple attention heads could work with a single next-token neuron.
Look into whether a single attention head could work with multiple next-token neurons.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for advancing their theoretical foundations and real-world applications. While the attention mechanism and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have been studied independently, their interactions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates how attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words. We propose a methodology to identify next-token neurons, find prompts that highly activate them, and determine the upstream attention heads responsible. We then generate and evaluate explanations for the activity of these attention heads in an automated manner. Our findings reveal that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly. This mechanism provides a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction. Our approach offers a foundation for further research into the intricate workings of LLMs and their impact on text generation and understanding.

papers.title: Promote, Suppress, Iterate: How Language Models Answer One-to-Many Factual Queries
papers.research_question: How do language models internally implement and integrate knowledge recall and repetition avoidance for one-to-many factual queries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a promote-then-suppress mechanism in language models for one-to-many factual queries, where attention propagates subject information and MLPs promote answers, then attention suppresses previous answers with MLPs amplifying the suppression signal.
papers.conclusion: LMs promote all answers and then suppress previously generated ones, using attention and MLPs to integrate subject and previous answer tokens for knowledge recall and repetition avoidance.
papers.key_findings:
LMs first promote all possible answers and then suppress previously generated ones.
Attention copies subject information to the last token, and MLPs use this information to promote answers.
Previous answer tokens are used for both knowledge recall (promoting new answers) and suppression.
Attention suppresses previous answers, and MLPs amplify this suppression signal.
The last token aggregates knowledge recall and suppression information to generate distinct answers.
papers.limitation:
Low accuracy due to long-tail entities, outdated datasets, and strict exact-match evaluation.
Analysis focuses only on correct cases, not on errors or unreliable signals.
future_direction: Investigate possible redundancies in how LMs encode knowledge across multiple tokens.
Examine patterns when LMs use unreliable signals or make errors.
papers.abstract: To answer one-to-many factual queries (e.g., listing cities of a country), a language model (LM) must simultaneously recall knowledge and avoid repeating previous answers. How are these two subtasks implemented and integrated internally? Across multiple datasets, models, and prompt templates, we identify a promote-then-suppress mechanism: the model first recalls all answers, and then suppresses previously generated ones. Specifically, LMs use both the subject and previous answer tokens to perform knowledge recall, with attention propagating subject information and MLPs promoting the answers. Then, attention attends to and suppresses previous answer tokens, while MLPs amplify the suppression signal. Our mechanism is corroborated by extensive experimental evidence: in addition to using early decoding and causal tracing, we analyze how components use different tokens by introducing both Token Lens, which decodes aggregated attention updates from specified tokens, and a knockout method that analyzes changes in MLP outputs after removing attention to specified tokens. Overall, we provide new insights into how LMs' internal components interact with different input tokens to support complex factual recall. Code is available at https://github.com/Lorenayannnnn/how-lms-answer-one-to-many-factual-queries.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval and Consolidation in Large Language Models through Function Tokens
papers.research_question: How is memory retrieved during inference and consolidated during pre-training in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Function Token Hypothesis to explain memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs, where function tokens activate predictive features during inference and drive feature learning during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Function Token Hypothesis, which explains how function tokens drive memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
During inference, a small set of function tokens activate the majority of the model's features.
Function tokens dynamically reactivate the most predictive features from the context to guide next-token prediction.
During pre-training, the prediction of content tokens following function tokens dominates the loss and drives feature expansion.
Pre-training initially focuses on learning to predict function tokens before learning content tokens.
Scaling model size primarily enhances the prediction of content tokens.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain how function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
future_direction: How function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
How post-training modifies activation patterns in function tokens.
The dynamics of feature formation and the underlying reason for the scale-free property of token-feature activation.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) stems from their ability to consolidate vast amounts of knowledge into the memory during pre-training and to retrieve it from the memory during inference, enabling advanced capabilities such as knowledge memorization, instruction-following and reasoning. However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. We provide extensive experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis. Using bipartite graph analysis, we show that a small number of function tokens activate the majority of features. Case studies further reveal how function tokens activate the most predictive features from context to direct next token prediction. We also find that during pre-training, the training loss is dominated by predicting the next content tokens following function tokens, which forces the function tokens to select the most predictive features from context.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Structured Context Recomposition for Large Language Models Using Probabilistic Layer Realignment
papers.research_question: Whether Structured Context Recomposition (SCR) enhances coherence retention in extended sequences without introducing significant computational penalties.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Structured Context Recomposition (SCR), a probabilistic layer realignment strategy that dynamically adjusts learned representations within transformer layers to maintain contextual coherence in extended sequences without significant computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: SCR effectively mitigates semantic drift and improves coherence retention in long sequences, offering a computationally viable alternative to existing methods that rely on external memory or retrieval.
papers.key_findings:
SCR maintains higher contextual consistency scores across extended sequences compared to baseline models.
SCR reduces semantic drift across iterative text generations, as indicated by a lower drift coefficient.
SCR maintains a more stable token entropy profile, reducing fluctuations that lead to context degradation.
SCR introduces smoother transitions of attention across transformer layers, reducing abrupt shifts in attention allocation.
