papers.key_findings:
Linear and MLP associative memories can store a number of associations proportional to their parameter count.
A one-layer transformer can achieve 100% accuracy on a synthetic factual recall task when either the total self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scale linearly with the number of facts.
The transformer exhibits sequential learning dynamics during training, with an initial 'hallucination' stage.
The storage constructions are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
papers.limitation: The linear associative memory construction requires the association function to be injective for optimal capacity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated an impressive ability to perform factual recall. Prior work has found that transformers trained on factual recall tasks can store information at a rate proportional to their parameter count. In our work, we show that shallow transformers can use a combination of associative memories to obtain such near optimal storage capacity. We begin by proving that the storage capacities of both linear and MLP associative memories scale linearly with parameter count. We next introduce a synthetic factual recall task, and prove that a transformer with a single layer of self-attention followed by an MLP can obtain 100% accuracy on the task whenever either the total number of self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scales (up to log factors) linearly with the number of facts. In particular, the transformer can trade off between using the value matrices or the MLP as an associative memory to store the dataset of facts. We complement these expressivity results with an analysis of the gradient flow trajectory of a simplified linear attention model trained on our factual recall task, where we show that the model exhibits sequential learning behavior.

papers.title: Multiple Streams of Knowledge Retrieval: Enriching and Recalling in Transformers
papers.research_question: When an LLM learns a new fact during finetuning, where does this information go? Are entities enriched with relation information immediately, or do models recall information just-in-time before a prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dynamic weight grafting, a method to localize finetuned knowledge in LLMs, and identifies two pathways for retrieving finetuned relation information: enrichment at the first entity and recall at the final token position.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic weight grafting is a novel method for localizing finetuned knowledge retrieval mechanisms in Transformer LLMs, revealing two pathways (enrichment and recall) and enabling precise localization of model components responsible for relation completion.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic weight grafting reveals two pathways for retrieving finetuned relation information: enrichment at the first entity and recall at the final token position.
Grafting only at the first entity or only at the last token can be sufficient to reproduce finetuned behavior, and both together nearly recover full finetuning performance.
The 'recall' pathway is localized to task-specific attention mechanisms at the first entity and the final token, and relation-specific extraction in the output projection matrix and feedforward networks of the final layers.
Grafting everything except the first entity and last token results in near-zero relation completion accuracy, showing these pathways are necessary.
The method provides a less destructive alternative to activation patching for localizing finetuned knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a synthetic knowledge retrieval task may limit generalization to more complex sentences or varied finetuning data.
Success is measured by top-k accuracy or token rank, which may not account for other ways models 'know' information that doesn't impact next token prediction.
Combinatorial explosion of possible grafting schemes means only a subset was explored.
Use of smaller models due to compute limitations; larger models may have different mechanisms.
future_direction: Explore the alternative entity enrichment pathway present in GPT2-XL and Pythia.
Extend to multi-hop relation settings.
Apply parameter-space interpretability techniques to the components identified as important for the task.
papers.abstract: When an LLM learns a new fact during finetuning (e.g., new movie releases, newly elected pope, etc.), where does this information go? Are entities enriched with relation information, or do models recall information just-in-time before a prediction? Or, are ``all of the above'' true with LLMs implementing multiple redundant heuristics? Existing localization approaches (e.g., activation patching) are ill-suited for this analysis because they usually \textit{replace} parts of the residual stream, thus overriding previous information. To fill this gap, we propose \emph{dynamic weight grafting}, a technique that selectively grafts weights from a finetuned model onto a pretrained model. Using this technique, we show two separate pathways for retrieving finetuned relation information: 1) ``enriching" the residual stream with relation information while processing the tokens that correspond to an entity (e.g., ``Zendaya'' in ``Zendaya co-starred with John David Washington'') and 2) ``recalling" this information at the final token position before generating a target fact. In some cases, models need information from both of these pathways to correctly generate finetuned facts while, in other cases, either the ``enrichment" or ``recall" pathway alone is sufficient. We localize the ``recall'' pathway to model components -- finding that ``recall" occurs via both task-specific attention mechanisms and an entity-specific extraction step in the feedforward networks of the final layers before the target prediction. By targeting model components and parameters, as opposed to just activations, we are able to understand the \textit{mechanisms} by which finetuned knowledge is retrieved during generation.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we control the knowledge selection behavior of large language models (LLMs) when there is a conflict between their parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in the hidden states of LLMs, enabling precise control over knowledge selection behavior during inference to resolve context-memory conflicts.
papers.conclusion: SPARE provides an effective and efficient training-free method for controlling knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, offering a promising approach to managing knowledge conflicts without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected by probing the residual stream of LLMs, with the strongest signal appearing in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively steers LLMs to use either contextual or parametric knowledge, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
The residual stream exhibits a significantly more skewed representation when the model uses contextual knowledge compared to when it uses parametric knowledge.
SPARE requires editing only a very small set of SAE features (e.g., less than 0.05% for Gemma2-9B) to achieve control.
The method is more effective at changing the model's behavior from using contextual to parametric knowledge than other inference-time methods.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on pre-trained SAEs, so it may not apply to models where such SAEs are unavailable or cannot be efficiently trained.
The experiments are conducted on specific open-domain QA tasks; generalization to other task types (e.g., complex reasoning, long-form generation) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in a binary fashion (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), whereas real-world decisions may require more nuanced approaches.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context -- this phenomenon, known as \emph{context-memory knowledge conflicts}, can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. Analysing the internal activations of LLMs, we find that they can internally register the signals of knowledge conflict at mid-layers. Such signals allow us to detect whether a knowledge conflict occurs and use \emph{inference-time} intervention strategies to resolve it. In this work, we propose \textsc{SpARE}, a \emph{training-free} representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to control the knowledge selection behaviour of LLMs. \textsc{SpARE} identifies the functional features that control the knowledge selection behaviours and applies them to edit the internal activations of LLMs at inference time. Our experimental results show that \textsc{SpARE} can effectively control the usage of either knowledge source to resolve knowledge conflict in open-domain question-answering tasks, surpassing existing representation engineering methods ($+10\%$) as well as contrastive decoding methods ($+15\%$).

papers.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do memorization and forgetting dynamics in language models change during training, and how do they depend on factors like model size, dataset size, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models memorize training data faster and forget less throughout training, with nouns and numbers being memorized more quickly than other parts of speech.
papers.conclusion: Memorization dynamics are a critical metric for understanding language model training, with larger models exhibiting faster memorization and less forgetting, highlighting the importance of analyzing memorization alongside cross-entropy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models memorize training data faster across various settings (causal and masked LM, different dataset sizes).
Larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting occurs.
Forgetting curves approach a baseline (the forgetting baseline), and this baseline increases with model scale, meaning larger models forget less.
Nouns and numbers are memorized much faster than other parts of speech, acting as unique identifiers for training examples.
Adding unique identifiers (like document IDs) to training examples increases memorization speed.
papers.limitation:
The exact memorization metric (Definition 1) ignores model confidence and does not normalize for duplication in the training set.
The focus on exact memorization may not capture all aspects of privacy, as it only considers verbatim output of sensitive information.
future_direction: Understanding the structure of the forgetting baseline, e.g., what types of tokens (parts of speech, synonyms, facts) are memorized in the baseline.
Analyzing memorization dynamics as a critical metric when scaling up language models, beyond just cross-entropy loss.
papers.abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process. We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

papers.title: What Should Embeddings Embed? Autoregressive Models Represent Latent Generating Distributions
papers.research_question: What should embeddings in autoregressive language models represent? The paper investigates whether embeddings correspond to predictive sufficient statistics of the data generating process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that embeddings from autoregressive language models correspond to predictive sufficient statistics, and empirically validates that these embeddings encode interpretable latent generating distributions (e.g., topic mixtures) in both synthetic and natural data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive language models learn to represent predictive sufficient statistics, which can be interpreted as latent generating distributions, providing a Bayesian inference perspective on what embeddings encode.
papers.key_findings:
In exchangeable models, transformer embeddings encode sufficient statistics of the data, such as the mean and variance of a Gaussian distribution.
In latent state models (e.g., HMMs), embeddings encode the posterior distribution over the next latent state given the observed sequence.
The embeddings generalize to out-of-distribution data and do not exhibit token memorization, indicating they capture statistical summaries rather than raw tokens.
In topic models (LDA), transformers encode topic mixtures, even when topics are only a sub-component of the data (as in HMM-LDA).
Pretrained LLMs (GPT-2, Llama 2, BERT) encode topic mixtures that align with those inferred by LDA on natural corpora (20Newsgroups and WikiText-103).
papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to extract latent structure from text. The embeddings from large language models have been shown to capture aspects of the syntax and semantics of language. But what should embeddings represent? We connect the autoregressive prediction objective to the idea of constructing predictive sufficient statistics to summarize the information contained in a sequence of observations, and use this connection to identify three settings where the optimal content of embeddings can be identified: independent identically distributed data, where the embedding should capture the sufficient statistics of the data; latent state models, where the embedding should encode the posterior distribution over states given the data; and discrete hypothesis spaces, where the embedding should reflect the posterior distribution over hypotheses given the data. We then conduct empirical probing studies to show that transformers encode these three kinds of latent generating distributions, and that they perform well in out-of-distribution cases and without token memorization in these settings.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: Transmuting prompts into weights
papers.research_question: Why do interventions like averaging contrastive activations or applying low-rank matrix updates succeed in controlling complex model behaviors? What is the underlying mathematical principle that connects a textual instruction to a specific change in a model’s weights or activations?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical foundation for activation steering and model editing by deriving a method to transmute prompts into reusable weight updates (thought vectors and matrices).
papers.conclusion: By bridging the gap between abstract transformer dynamics and tangible weight updates, this work provides a robust foundation for the next generation of efficient, mathematically grounded model editing techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Thought vectors and matrices can be derived from token patches via averaging and least-squares optimization.
This provides a theoretical explanation for heuristic activation steering (e.g., contrastive averaging) and low-rank model editing (e.g., ROME).
Empirical validation shows thought patches can specialize models for tasks like arithmetic, detoxification, translation, and knowledge retrieval, achieving performance comparable to full context prompting.
New knowledge can be integrated via thought patches, but performance degrades with dictionary size and query mismatch.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with larger dictionary sizes and when retrieval queries differ from those used during patch computation, indicating overfitting to prompt structures.
future_direction: Developing more robust regularization schemes to prevent overfitting to prompt structures.
papers.abstract: A growing body of research has demonstrated that the behavior of large language models can be effectively controlled at inference time by directly modifying their internal states, either through vector additions to their activations or through updates to their weight matrices. These techniques, while powerful, are often guided by empirical heuristics, such as deriving steering vectors from the average activations of contrastive prompts. This work provides a theoretical foundation for these interventions, explaining how they emerge from the fundamental computations of the transformer architecture. Building on the recent finding that a prompt's influence can be mathematically mapped to token-dependent implicit weight updates (Dherin et. al, 2025), we derive a principled method for condensing this information into token-independent thought vectors and thought matrices. These constructs provide a theoretical explanation for existing vector-and-matrix-based model editing techniques and offer a direct, computationally-grounded method for transmuting textual input into reusable weight updates.

papers.title: Representation and Pre-Activation of Lexical-Semantic Knowledge in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How closely do the intermediate layers of LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge, both before and after the target word is presented?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models (GPT-2) are better at capturing semantic knowledge, especially attributive features, than LSTM models, and both models retain rich semantic representations of a concept after it has been presented.
papers.conclusion: The transformer model is much better at capturing attributive features than the LSTM model, whilst both models are able to retain rich semantic representations of the concept after the concept has been given to the network.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer models (GPT-2) outperform LSTM models in capturing semantic knowledge, particularly for attributive features.
Both models retain semantic information about a concept after the word is presented, with earlier layers performing better in the 'after' condition.
The final layer of both models shows a performance drop in the 'after' condition, likely due to increased context specificity.
In the 'before' condition (predicting the word), later layers are more representative of the upcoming word's semantics.
GPT-2's after representations are more effective in lower layers, while JLM's after representations are better in the first layer.
papers.limitation:
The feature pooling method may not fully capture context-specific representations, especially in later layers where representations become more context-specific.
Linear probes may not fully capture the information encoded in the representations; failure to decode a property does not mean it is not encoded.
papers.abstract: Neural network language models have the ability to capture the contextualised meanings of words in a sentence by dynamically evolving a representation of the linguistic input in a manner evocative of human language comprehension. While researchers have been able to analyse whether key linguistic regularities are adequately characterised by these evolving representations, determining whether they activate lexico-semantic knowledge similarly to humans remains challenging. In this paper, we perform a systematic analysis of how closely the intermediate layers from LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge. Furthermore, in order to make more meaningful comparisons with theories of human language comprehension in psycholinguistics, we focus on two key stages where the meaning of a particular target word may arise: immediately before the word's presentation to the model (comparable to forward inferencing), and immediately after the word token has been input into the network. Our results indicate that the transformer models are better at capturing semantic knowledge relating to lexical concepts, both during word prediction and when retention is required.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Latent Positional Information is in the Self-Attention Variance of Transformer Language Models Without Positional Embeddings
papers.research_question: Where is positional information stored in transformer language models without positional embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without positional embeddings inherently encode strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance, an effect that persists after pre-training.
papers.conclusion: Positional information is encoded in the self-attention variance of transformer language models without positional embeddings, justifying their removal for more efficient pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
The variance of the self-attention output in a randomly initialized transformer language model without positional embeddings decreases as the token position increases, providing latent positional information.
This variance shrinkage effect is attributed to the interaction between the causal attention mask and the transformer architecture.
The derived variance properties for the randomly initialized model are also observed in the lower layers of a fully pre-trained model.
BERT without positional embeddings fails to encode positional information because its bidirectional attention leads to constant variance across all positions.
Predicting the position of later tokens is more challenging due to the plateauing of variance for larger positions.
papers.limitation: The analysis relies on assumptions of a randomly initialized and frozen TLM and randomly sampled input tokens, which do not hold for human languages and pre-trained TLMs.
future_direction: Analyze the training dynamics of a TLM to understand the model parameter distribution after pre-training.
Use Zipf's law or n-gram language models to quantify the degree of input token duplication in human languages for a more accurate variance estimate.
papers.abstract: The use of positional embeddings in transformer language models is widely accepted. However, recent research has called into question the necessity of such embeddings. We further extend this inquiry by demonstrating that a randomly initialized and frozen transformer language model, devoid of positional embeddings, inherently encodes strong positional information through the shrinkage of self-attention variance. To quantify this variance, we derive the underlying distribution of each step within a transformer layer. Through empirical validation using a fully pretrained model, we show that the variance shrinkage effect still persists after extensive gradient updates. Our findings serve to justify the decision to discard positional embeddings and thus facilitate more efficient pretraining of transformer language models.

papers.title: Prompt Perturbation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are the outputs from RAG-based LLMs affected by slightly different inputs (prompt perturbations), and how can such perturbations be detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gradient Guided Prompt Perturbation (GGPP), a method to generate adversarial prefixes that mislead RAG-based LLMs to retrieve wrong passages and generate factually wrong answers, and proposes ACT probe for efficient detection of such perturbations.
papers.conclusion: RAG-based LLMs are vulnerable to prompt perturbations, and the proposed ACT probe provides an efficient defense by detecting such perturbations.
papers.key_findings:
GGPP can successfully perturb prompts to cause retrieval of wrong passages with high success rates.
The ACT probe is effective in detecting perturbations with fewer parameters compared to SATe.
RAG-based LLMs are vulnerable to prompt perturbations even with instructions to ignore irrelevant information.
papers.abstract: The robustness of large language models (LLMs) becomes increasingly important as their use rapidly grows in a wide range of domains. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is considered as a means to improve the trustworthiness of text generation from LLMs. However, how the outputs from RAG-based LLMs are affected by slightly different inputs is not well studied. In this work, we find that the insertion of even a short prefix to the prompt leads to the generation of outputs far away from factually correct answers. We systematically evaluate the effect of such prefixes on RAG by introducing a novel optimization technique called Gradient Guided Prompt Perturbation (GGPP). GGPP achieves a high success rate in steering outputs of RAG-based LLMs to targeted wrong answers. It can also cope with instructions in the prompts requesting to ignore irrelevant context. We also exploit LLMs' neuron activation difference between prompts with and without GGPP perturbations to give a method that improves the robustness of RAG-based LLMs through a highly effective detector trained on neuron activation triggered by GGPP generated prompts. Our evaluation on open-sourced LLMs demonstrates the effectiveness of our methods.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Unsupervised Real-Time Hallucination Detection based on the Internal States of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can hallucinations in large language models be detected in real-time using the models' internal states, without requiring manual annotations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIND, an unsupervised framework for real-time hallucination detection using the internal states of LLMs, and HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs.
papers.conclusion: MIND is an effective unsupervised method for real-time hallucination detection, and the HELM benchmark facilitates future research in this area.
papers.key_findings:
MIND outperforms existing hallucination detection methods in terms of AUC and correlation.
MIND is highly efficient, taking only about 3% of the LLM's response generation time for detection.
Customized training data generated by the same LLM significantly improves hallucination detection performance.
The method is broadly effective across a variety of LLMs.
Using the contextualized embedding of the last token of the last layer is effective for hallucination detection.
papers.limitation: Detecting hallucinations using only the internal states of LLMs may not be as accurate as combining internal states with generated text.
future_direction: Integrating internal states of LLMs with generated text for improved hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) refer to the phenomenon of LLMs producing responses that are coherent yet factually inaccurate. This issue undermines the effectiveness of LLMs in practical applications, necessitating research into detecting and mitigating hallucinations of LLMs. Previous studies have mainly concentrated on post-processing techniques for hallucination detection, which tend to be computationally intensive and limited in effectiveness due to their separation from the LLM's inference process. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MIND, an unsupervised training framework that leverages the internal states of LLMs for real-time hallucination detection without requiring manual annotations. Additionally, we present HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs, featuring diverse LLM outputs and the internal states of LLMs during their inference process. Our experiments demonstrate that MIND outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in hallucination detection.

papers.title: InnerThoughts: Disentangling Representations and Predictions in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve large language model accuracy on multiple-choice question-answering tasks by leveraging hidden states from all layers, thereby disentangling representational abilities from predictive abilities?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes InnerThoughts, a method that trains a small neural network predictor on the hidden states from all layers at the last token position to predict answers for multiple-choice questions, improving accuracy over calibration baselines at a fraction of the computational cost of fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: InnerThoughts provides an effective and computationally efficient method for improving LLM performance on multiple-choice QA by disentangling representations from predictions, offering a cheaper alternative to adapter-based fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
InnerThoughts achieves substantial accuracy gains over direct prompting and calibration baselines on multiple-choice QA benchmarks, sometimes approaching the performance of supervised fine-tuning.
The method is most beneficial on datasets where the base LLM has low confidence in its answers, such as those requiring non-linguistic skills like algebra (AQuA) or visualization (HellaSwag).
Using hidden states from all layers provides more useful information for prediction than using only the final layer's hidden state or logits.
InnerThoughts is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass through the frozen LLM during training, achieving on average 35% of the gains of QLoRA fine-tuning at 16% of the cost.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) contain substantial factual knowledge which is commonly elicited by multiple-choice question-answering prompts. Internally, such models process the prompt through multiple transformer layers, building varying representations of the problem within its hidden states. Ultimately, however, only the hidden state corresponding to the final layer and token position are used to predict the answer label. In this work, we propose instead to learn a small separate neural network predictor module on a collection of training questions, that take the hidden states from all the layers at the last temporal position as input and outputs predictions. In effect, such a framework disentangles the representational abilities of LLMs from their predictive abilities. On a collection of hard benchmarks, our method achieves considerable improvements in performance, sometimes comparable to supervised fine-tuning procedures, but at a fraction of the computational cost.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Tokens in Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of latent tokens (jointly predicted but undecoded tokens) in diffusion models, and can introducing them into autoregressive models improve performance on reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Latent tokens (jointly predicted but undecoded tokens) are a key mechanism in diffusion models for reasoning tasks, and introducing them into autoregressive models via multi-token prediction improves performance.
papers.conclusion: Latent tokens are a key mechanism for reasoning in diffusion models, and they can be successfully introduced into autoregressive models to improve performance on tasks requiring global coherence.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating joint prediction in diffusion models (SIDM) speeds inference but degrades performance, indicating the importance of latent tokens.
Increasing the number of latent tokens in diffusion models (via modulation) improves accuracy on reasoning tasks and reduces perplexity in language modeling.
Introducing latent tokens into autoregressive models via multi-token prediction (AR-MTP) substantially improves reasoning performance, closing the gap with diffusion models.
The number of latent tokens provides a controllable trade-off between inference speed and sample quality.
Latent tokens are a general mechanism for improving performance on tasks requiring global coherence or lookahead.
papers.limitation: The scaling of performance with latent tokens may depend on the training data distribution, which is not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate when latent token scaling emerges in different training data distributions.
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have recently become competitive with autoregressive models for language modeling, even outperforming them on reasoning tasks requiring planning and global coherence, but they require more computation at inference time. We trace this trade-off to a key mechanism: diffusion models are trained to jointly predict a distribution over all unknown tokens, including those that will not actually be decoded in the current step. Ablating this joint prediction yields faster inference but degrades performance, revealing that accurate prediction at the decoded position relies on joint reasoning about the distribution of undecoded tokens. We interpret these as latent tokens and introduce a method for modulating their number, demonstrating empirically that this enables a smooth tradeoff between inference speed and sample quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that latent tokens can be introduced into autoregressive models through an auxiliary multi-token prediction objective, yielding substantial improvements on the same reasoning tasks where they have traditionally struggled. Our results suggest that latent tokens, while arising naturally in diffusion, represent a general mechanism for improving performance on tasks requiring global coherence or lookahead.

papers.title: On the Semantic and Syntactic Information Encoded in Proto-Tokens for One-Step Text Reconstruction
papers.research_question: What semantic and syntactic information do proto-tokens encode in one-step text reconstruction with frozen LLMs, and how can semantic structure be imposed on them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in one-step text reconstruction with frozen LLMs, the m-token encodes more semantic information than the e-token, and relational distillation can impose semantic structure on proto-tokens while maintaining reconstruction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that proto-tokens in one-step reconstruction encode both semantic and syntactic information, and relational distillation can effectively impose semantic structure, supporting future non-autoregressive seq2seq systems.
papers.key_findings:
Under unconstrained optimization, the m-token tends to capture semantic information more strongly than the e-token.
Anchor-based regularization that forces e toward a teacher embedding introduces a sharp trade-off between similarity and reconstruction accuracy.
Relational distillation can transfer batch-level semantic relations into the proto-token space without sacrificing reconstruction performance.
Proto-tokens encode syntactic information as well, as shown by clustering experiments.
Attention patterns indicate that the model actively uses the e-token during decoding.
future_direction: Building an explicit proto-token predictor for controlled generation.
Quantifying syntactic vs. semantic disentanglement.
Improving identifiability and stability of proto-token representations across optimization runs.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive large language models (LLMs) generate text token-by-token, requiring n forward passes to produce a sequence of length n. Recent work, Exploring the Latent Capacity of LLMs for One-Step Text Reconstruction (Mezentsev and Oseledets), shows that frozen LLMs can reconstruct hundreds of tokens from only two learned proto-tokens in a single forward pass, suggesting a path beyond the autoregressive paradigm. In this paper, we study what information these proto-tokens encode and how they behave under reconstruction and controlled constraints. We perform a series of experiments aimed at disentangling semantic and syntactic content in the two proto-tokens, analyzing stability properties of the e-token, and visualizing attention patterns to the e-token during reconstruction. Finally, we test two regularization schemes for "imposing" semantic structure on the e-token using teacher embeddings, including an anchor-based loss and a relational distillation objective. Our results indicate that the m-token tends to capture semantic information more strongly than the e-token under standard optimization; anchor-based constraints trade off sharply with reconstruction accuracy; and relational distillation can transfer batch-level semantic relations into the proto-token space without sacrificing reconstruction quality, supporting the feasibility of future non-autoregressive seq2seq systems that predict proto-tokens as an intermediate representation.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: In Machina N400: Pinpointing Where a Causal Language Model Detects Semantic Violations
papers.research_question: At which computational depth does a transformer first register a semantic anomaly, and does this temporal pattern align with the timing of the human N400 response?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that semantic anomaly detection in the transformer model Phi-2 emerges in mid-to-late layers, with decoding accuracy peaking around layer 22, and reveals a biphasic representational geometry with initial expansion followed by compression, paralleling human N400 dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that both artificial and biological language systems may postpone semantic anomaly detection until sufficient context is integrated, with parallels to human N400 responses, though mechanisms may differ.
papers.key_findings:
Decoding accuracy for semantic violations peaks at layer 22 with AUC 0.723, and is significant only in layers 18-30.
Participation ratio analysis shows that violations initially increase dimensionality in early layers (1-6), then decrease below control levels after layer 12.
The late emergence of anomaly detection suggests semantic integration occurs after syntactic processing, similar to human language comprehension.
papers.limitation:
Results are from a single model (Phi-2) and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
Stimuli have fixed violation position, which could allow the model to exploit positional regularity.
Only participation ratio was used for geometry analysis; other measures might reveal additional structure.
Statistical robustness relies on five-fold cross-validation; larger corpora could improve generality.
Linear logistic regression was the primary probe; non-linear methods might provide further insights.
future_direction: Replicate analysis in larger autoregressive LMs and bidirectional encoders to test architecture generality.
Randomize violation position and introduce graded expectancy manipulations in stimuli.
Use complementary geometry metrics like intrinsic dimensionality or manifold capacity.
papers.abstract: How and where does a transformer notice that a sentence has gone semantically off the rails? To explore this question, we evaluated the causal language model (phi-2) using a carefully curated corpus, with sentences that concluded plausibly or implausibly. Our analysis focused on the hidden states sampled at each model layer. To investigate how violations are encoded, we utilized two complementary probes. First, we conducted a per-layer detection using a linear probe. Our findings revealed that a simple linear decoder struggled to distinguish between plausible and implausible endings in the lowest third of the model's layers. However, its accuracy sharply increased in the middle blocks, reaching a peak just before the top layers. Second, we examined the effective dimensionality of the encoded violation. Initially, the violation widens the representational subspace, followed by a collapse after a mid-stack bottleneck. This might indicate an exploratory phase that transitions into rapid consolidation. Taken together, these results contemplate the idea of alignment with classical psycholinguistic findings in human reading, where semantic anomalies are detected only after syntactic resolution, occurring later in the online processing sequence.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: Extracting Paragraphs from LLM Token Activations
papers.research_question: How much do large language models plan the content of a paragraph at its beginning, and can single-token activations encode this information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that single-token activations, specifically the double newline token, encode contextual information about upcoming paragraphs, and patching these activations can transfer this information, revealing the model's capacity for planning ahead.
papers.conclusion: A single token encodes a substantial amount of contextual information about the forthcoming section, with most information contained in the first two tokens of generation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights indicate that the model attends primarily to tokens within the same paragraph during text generation.
Cosine similarity of attention outputs shows that paragraph structure is encoded in early layers, with distinctions between paragraphs diminishing in final layers.
Patching activations from the double newline token can transfer contextual information to generate text semantically similar to the original paragraph.
Transferred generations outperform neutral baselines even when hints are provided, with statistical significance.
Most of the contextual information is contained in the first two tokens of generation, but not all.
papers.limitation:
The framework is designed specifically for autoregressive models and does not apply to word2word models.
The study is an experimental investigation rather than a comprehensive solution, and methods are not foolproof or suited for high-stakes models.
Experiments were conducted using only a specific language model (Gemma 2), though findings are expected to generalize to other transformer-based models.
future_direction: Explore applying the approach to cohesive texts without abrupt context switches.
Extend the framework to predict further sections ahead, not just the immediate next paragraph.
papers.abstract: Generative large language models (LLMs) excel in natural language processing tasks, yet their inner workings remain underexplored beyond token-level predictions. This study investigates the degree to which these models decide the content of a paragraph at its onset, shedding light on their contextual understanding. By examining the information encoded in single-token activations, specifically the "\textbackslash n\textbackslash n" double newline token, we demonstrate that patching these activations can transfer significant information about the context of the following paragraph, providing further insights into the model's capacity to plan ahead.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations.
